content: Fungi are organisms that form noticeable fruiting bodies, which can sometimes resemble plants like mosses. Both fungi and plants possess a cell wall, a feature absent in the Animal Kingdom. However, fungi are now classified as a separate kingdom, distinct from both plants and animals, with evidence suggesting they diverged from these groups approximately one billion years ago. Numerous studies have identified unique morphological, biochemical, and genetic traits in fungi, clearly distinguishing them from other kingdoms. For these reasons, fungi are placed in their own kingdom. Unlike most plants, fungi lack the ability to synthesize organic carbon through chlorophyll-based photosynthesis. Instead, fungi, like animals and some bacteria, store carbohydrates as glycogen, whereas plants store reduced carbon as starch. The cell wall of many fungal species is primarily composed of chitin, a nitrogen-containing carbohydrate also found in some animals, such as insects and crustaceans. In contrast, plant cell walls are predominantly made of cellulose. A defining feature of fungal cells is their growth as hyphae, which are microscopic filaments measuring 2–10 microns in diameter and extending up to several centimeters in length. These hyphae collectively form the fungal mycelium. Some fungi, such as yeasts, grow as single oval-shaped cells, resembling unicellular algae and protists. Unlike many plants, most fungi lack an efficient vascular system, such as xylem or phloem, for long-distance transport of water and nutrients. However, some fungi, like Armillaria, have evolved rhizomorphs or mycelial cords, which are functionally similar to plant roots but morphologically distinct. Fungi share certain characteristics with plants, such as the presence of vacuoles in their cells and a similar pathway for terpene biosynthesis using mevalonic acid and pyrophosphate as biochemical precursors. However, plants also utilize an additional terpene biosynthesis pathway in their chloroplasts, which is absent in fungi. Ancestral traits shared among fungi include chitinous cell walls and heterotrophy by absorption. A unique feature of fungi, not found in other eukaryotes but shared with some bacteria, is the biosynthesis of the amino acid L-lysine via the α-aminoadipate pathway. Like plants, fungi produce a wide array of secondary metabolites that serve as defensive compounds or aid in niche adaptation. However, the biochemical pathways for synthesizing similar or even identical compounds often differ significantly between fungi and plants. The earliest organisms with features typical of fungi date back to approximately 1.2 billion years ago during the Proterozoic era. However, fungal fossils become more common and uncontroversial in the early Devonian period, particularly in the Rhynie chert. Although traditionally included in botany curricula and textbooks, fungi are now considered more closely related to animals than to plants. They are grouped with animals in the monophyletic clade of opisthokonts. For much of the Paleozoic Era, fungi appear to have been aquatic organisms, resembling modern chytrids with flagellum-bearing spores. The early fossil record of fungi is notably fragmentary. Fungi likely colonized land during the Cambrian period, long before land plants. Following the Permian-Triassic extinction event, a fungal spike was observed, initially interpreted as an extraordinary abundance of fungal spores in sediments from this period. This suggested fungi were the dominant life form during this time, accounting for nearly 100% of the fossil record from this period. However, the relative proportion of fungal spores compared to algal spores is difficult to assess, and the spike was not observed worldwide or consistently at the Permian-Triassic boundary. Molecular phylogenetic analyses support a monophyletic origin of fungi. The taxonomy of fungi is in a state of constant flux, particularly due to recent DNA-based research. These phylogenetic analyses often overturn older classifications based on less precise methods, such as morphological features and biological species concepts derived from experimental matings. There is no universally accepted system at higher taxonomic levels, and frequent name changes occur at all levels, from species upwards. Efforts are underway among fungal researchers to establish and promote a unified and more consistent nomenclature. Fungal species can also have multiple scientific names depending on their life cycle and mode of reproduction (sexual or asexual). Websites like Index Fungorum and ITIS provide preferred, up-to-date names with cross-references to older synonyms, though they do not always agree with each other. The major divisions (phyla) of fungi are classified primarily based on their sexual reproductive structures. Currently, seven fungal divisions are proposed: 1. Chytridiomycota: Commonly known as chytrids, these fungi are ubiquitous with a worldwide distribution. Chytrids produce zoospores capable of active movement through aqueous environments using a single flagellum. Due to this flagellum, some taxonomists previously classified them as protists. Ribosomal subunit analyses suggest that chytrids are a basal fungal group, divergent from other fungal divisions, consisting of four major clades with evidence for paraphyly or possibly polyphyly. 2. Blastocladiomycota: Previously considered a clade within Chytridiomycota, recent molecular data and ultrastructural characteristics place Blastocladiomycota as a sister clade to Zygomycota, Glomeromycota, and Dikarya (Ascomycota and Basidiomycota). Blastocladiomycetes are fungi that act as saprotrophs and parasites of all eukaryotic groups. They undergo sporic meiosis, unlike their close relatives, chytrids, which mostly exhibit zygotic meiosis. 3. Neocallimastigomycota: Initially placed within Chytridiomycota, members of this small phylum are anaerobic organisms living in the digestive systems of large herbivorous mammals and possibly in other terrestrial and aquatic environments. They lack mitochondria but contain hydrogenosomes of mitochondrial origin. Like chytrids, neocallimastigomycetes form zoospores that are posteriorly uniflagellate or polyflagellate.
